verified_findings.claim: The NIHK overseas-source catalog identifies a substantial US Embassy classified folder titled '363.11-So, Min Ho Trial. 1952' and explicitly lists three Korean National Assembly special-investigation reports plus a trial summary and USIS courtroom/scene photographs.
verified_findings.significance: This converts a generic lead into a document-level target set with named report numbers and provenance.

verified_findings.claim: Special Investigation Report No.1 is dated 1952-05-09 and names six Assembly investigators: Yu Hong, Kim Gwang-jun, Jo Sun, Kim Jeong-gi, Jo Jeong-hun and Lee Seok-gi; the catalog says it contains introduction, incident outline, witness investigation and supporting documents.
verified_findings.caution: Catalog metadata verifies existence/composition; report text itself still needs direct transcription.

verified_findings.claim: The same folder separately identifies Report No.2 as So Min-ho's statement and Report No.3 as the prosecution investigation, providing an unusually clean adversarial source triad inside one archival folder.

A July 1 contemporaneous report records a death sentence against So Min-ho and a 250,000 won fine against Seo Won-ryong, with presiding judge Park Dong-gyun stating unanimous guilt under Martial Law Act Article 16 and Penal Code Article 199 for So.
verified_findings.caution: This is the July 1 court-martial judgment as contemporaneously reported, not the end of the later review/civil-court chain.

verified_findings.claim: The July 1 hearing was the fifteenth hearing and was observed by US Embassy officer Richard W. Petrie, British legation personnel, UN Commission personnel and AP/UP reporters, creating independent-observer leads for the trial record.

The May 10 prosecution statement identifies Jeong Jin-dong as National Assembly Interior/Public-Security specialist and names Seo Won-ryong, Kim Cheo-jung and Lee Jong-seok as members of So's accompanying security party on the local-election inspection trip.
verified_findings.caution: These are actor identities in the prosecution narrative; individual conduct still requires comparison with Assembly reports and defense statement.

verified_findings.claim: Presidential Archives-hosted scholarship places the Assembly release resolution on May 14 and So's release immediately before the May 25 emergency-martial-law turn, strengthening the need to encode release, re-arrest and court-martial transfer as distinct subevents.
verified_findings.caution: Original Assembly resolution and martial-law re-arrest order remain the preferred primary targets.

verified_findings.claim: AKS confirms So Min-ho as a durable independent political node, not merely an incident participant: second-National-Assembly member, later fifth-National-Assembly vice speaker, party leader and multi-term legislator.

adversarial_checks: The May 10 prosecution claim that the case was nonpolitical must be tested against the Assembly special-investigation reports and later judicial findings.
The Assembly special-investigation reports are not automatically neutral merely because they are parliamentary documents; member positions and evidence attachments must be inspected.
Catalog metadata establishes report existence and structure, not the truth of each report's factual conclusions.
The July 1 death sentence is not the final disposition; later review and civil-court proceedings must remain separate nodes.
The use of Martial Law Act Article 16 must be checked against the exact 1952 statutory text and jurisdictional basis rather than inferred from the press report alone.
Seo Won-ryong's family relationship to So Min-ho cannot substitute for evidence of his conduct; Report No.2/3 and judgment are required.
The temporal proximity of So's release, emergency martial law and re-arrest does not by itself prove the martial-law declaration was issued principally to re-arrest him.
Later descriptions of the shooting as an assassination attempt conflict with the May 10 prosecution narrative; both need comparison against witness statements and physical evidence.
A later political career and independence-movement record do not determine guilt or innocence in the 1952 shooting.
Foreign observers' attendance proves scrutiny, not their assessment; their dispatches must be retrieved before using them as corroboration.
